Who I am

About Me

I am a sophomore Bioengineering student at the University of Pittsburgh's Frederick Honors College, pursuing a minor in Industrial Engineering. My interests lie at the intersection of healthcare innovation, biomechanics, and human-centered design. Through coursework in engineering design, physics, chemistry, calculus, and professional communication, I have built a strong foundation in both technical problem-solving and clear communication.

My experiences have helped me connect engineering with real-world impact. This past summer, I interned at StackGen, where I managed a dataset of over 177,000 incident records, wrote Python scripts to collect and merge data, and co-authored the State of Reliability 2026 report. I also serve as an Engineering Peer Leader at Pitt's Swanson School of Engineering, co-facilitating weekly recitation sections and mentoring first-year engineering students on academics, time management, and campus life. I have additionally explored biotechnology through hands-on lab programs involving PCR, gel electrophoresis, CRISPR, and ELISA. As I continue studying bioengineering, my goal is to design practical, accessible solutions — particularly in areas like fall prevention, musculoskeletal health, and patient mobility — that meaningfully improve people's quality of life.

Projects

ENGR 0717 - Honors Foundations of Engineering Design

Foam Core Enclosure

Overview: For this design challenge, I created a small foam core enclosure using introductory prototyping techniques. The goal was to build an enclosure under one gallon in volume, then exchange prototypes with a partner and modify their design by adding a hidden compartment.

Process: I designed my enclosure to look like a gift box with a red exterior and ribbon-like details. After handing it off, I received my partner's prototype and thought creatively about where a secret compartment could be added without making it obvious.

Outcome: The final product was a decorative enclosure with a hidden compartment. This project helped me practice rapid prototyping, spatial reasoning, and designing around both form and function.

Skills: Foam core prototyping · Hand fabrication · Measurement · Hidden feature design · Iterative thinking

ENGR 0717 - Honors Foundations of Engineering Design

Timber Composites Design

Overview: My team designed and built a wooden chair that had to maximize strength while minimizing material usage and staying within a set budget. The chair needed to support weight during load testing.

Process: We used longer back legs with a tongue-and-groove approach, added a cross-wood support using a half-lap joint, and reinforced front leg connections. Our Minion-inspired design balanced aesthetics with structural integrity.

Outcome: The final chair held 140 pounds — matching our predicted maximum load — at a cost-to-weight ratio of ₣2.83 per pound supported. Small design choices in joint selection and load distribution strongly affected performance.

Skills: Woodworking · Joint design · Structural support · Budgeting · Load testing · Design iteration

ENGR 0717 - Honors Foundations of Engineering Design

Robotic Rube Goldberg

Overview: My team designed a Candy Land-themed robotic Rube Goldberg machine that completed a task using a single initial impulse, with at least five connected mechanisms including an Arduino-controlled mechatronic component.

Process: The sequence ran through dice, dominoes, a ball launcher, PVC pipes, a back-and-forth ramp, and a pulley. A pressure sensor triggered a DC motor that dispensed candy at the end. I also contributed heavily to the colorful Candy Land visual design.

Outcome: The machine completed the full sequence successfully. The project taught me how mechanical energy transfers through a system and how constant troubleshooting is central to engineering design.

Skills: Mechanical design · Arduino · Sensors & motors · Energy transfer · Troubleshooting · Visual design

ENGR 0717 - Honors Foundations of Engineering Design

Designing Flavors and Scaling Parties

Overview: My team created an Excel-based tool to scale a vegetable stir fry recipe from 4 servings to 1,000 guests, managing ingredient quantities, labor needs, production timing, and food temperature safety.

Process: The model included recipe scaling, a production schedule (12 PM–8 PM), labor planning, and temperature control. I contributed to the labor planner, management functionality, and error-checking. We identified noodle boiling and stir fry cooking as the main bottlenecks.

Outcome: The final model showed how a small recipe becomes a large-scale production plan, demonstrating how engineering tools like spreadsheets, scheduling, and workflow analysis apply in real-world event planning.

Skills: Excel modeling · Recipe scaling · Workflow planning · Labor allocation · Bottleneck analysis · Operations management

Cornerstone — ENGR 0717

Low-Resource
Compression Therapy

My team designed Thera-Comp, a low-resource compression therapy system meant to make compression therapy more accessible. Compression therapy improves circulation, reduces swelling, and supports recovery — but commercial systems like NormaTec can be expensive and difficult to access in low-resource settings.

We interviewed occupational and physical therapists, a physical therapy student, and NCAA and competitive athletes to understand real needs. Therapists emphasized safety, comfort, and a flush fit against the limb. Athletes emphasized portability. These interviews helped us focus on a design that was affordable, portable, and not overly bulky.

Our design used an external fabric sleeve and an internal air bladder made from a large beach ball, cut and heat-sealed with a hair straightener. The system included fittings for inflation, pressure monitoring, and pressure release. We chose manual control over electronic inflation to keep costs low and stay true to the low-resource goal.

The final prototype demonstrated a low-cost alternative to commercial compression systems using everyday materials with no electronics required. This project helped me connect bioengineering, user-centered design, global health, and frugal innovation.

Skills: Bioengineering design · User interviews · Medical device prototyping · Low-resource engineering · Pressure safety · Global health design

Project Poster

Design Expo

At the end of the project, we presented Thera-Comp at the University of Pittsburgh Engineering Design Expo. Our team set up a table with our final prototype, project poster, and supporting materials so visitors could see how the device worked and understand the design process behind it. We used the display to explain the problem we were addressing, show the low-cost materials we used, and discuss how our design could make compression therapy more accessible in low-resource communities. This experience helped us practice communicating a technical project to a broad audience, including students, faculty, and visitors who may not have had prior knowledge of compression therapy.

Community

Teaching Public Health to
Elementary Students

For my ENGR 0717 service project, I created and delivered a public health presentation to a fourth-grade class at Waxpool Elementary School in Ashburn, Virginia on March 12, 2026. The lesson reached 25 students and was designed as a meaningful service project for a community outside my immediate social network.

I created a visual presentation called "Public Health: More Than Just Germs" covering how germs spread, clean water, safe food, healthy habits, and public health careers. I originally planned a glitter activity to model germ spread, but adjusted the project to include questions throughout the lesson and a true/false game at the end — keeping students engaged while checking for understanding.

The lesson was highly interactive. Students participated throughout, answered questions, and almost the entire class raised their hands when asked about careers they might be interested in. The true/false game confirmed that students understood how germs spread and how they can help protect their classroom community.

Skills: Public speaking · Service learning · Health education · Lesson planning · Audience-centered communication · Community impact

Arduino

I installed and configured the Arduino IDE for an ELEGOO UNO R3 connected through COM3, then completed Lessons 1–15 of the ELEGOO Super Starter Kit tutorials. Through hands-on breadboard circuits and Arduino sketches, I explored LEDs and RGB lighting, digital inputs, active and passive buzzers, a tilt switch, servo motors, distance sensing, temperature and humidity sensing, an analog joystick, infrared remote control, an LCD screen, and a thermometer. I practiced wiring electronic components, working with Arduino libraries, uploading code, and using the Serial Monitor to observe and troubleshoot sensor readings.

Skill

Soldering

I used soldering to build a small digital clock from a kit. Following the assembly instructions, I soldered the components onto the circuit board in order from shortest to tallest, trimming the leads after each group, and mounted the integrated circuit in a socket so it could be fitted last. I then checked each joint for missed connections, short circuits, and cold solder joints, and fit the finished board into its clear case.
